title: Trans people should use hospital spaces according to biological sex, NHS England says
description: Trans patients should be cared for on single-sex hospital wards or bays that align with their biological sex rather than their gender identity, accord
body: Trans patients should be cared for on single-sex hospital wards or bays that align with their biological sex rather than their gender identity, according to new NHS England (NHSE) guidance.It says when this is not "clinically appropriate" then alternative arrangements should be made and the dignity and safety of all patients should be maintained.The guidance also says staff facilities should be used by people based on their biological sex, while trusts should ensure enough alternatives to single-sex facilities, such as single-occupancy toilets, are offered.Previous NHSE guidance suggested patients and staff could be accommodated on wards or use facilities based on their gender identity.That meant that a trans woman – a biological male who identifies as a woman – could have chosen to be on a women's ward, or a trans man – a biological female who identifies as a man – could have opted for a men's ward.That guidance was withdrawn following the Supreme Court ruling in April 2025 that under equality law the term "sex" means biological sex and "woman" refers to a biological woman. The judgment said for a space or service to be single sex it should only allow those of the same biological sex to use it.Also under the new guidance issued on Thursday, NHSE emphasised that in order to avoid discriminating against trans people they should be offered gender neutral spaces.But the guidance also says decisions may have to be made on a case-by-case basis and must ensure clinical needs are met.It also makes clear that there are circumstances where clinical need is the overriding priority, including on emergency units and urgent care settings.In addition to the patient document of the guidance, NHSE has published advice for trusts on how to organise changing rooms, toilets and other single-sex facilities for staff.Again, it says they should be used by people based on their biological sex, not their gender identity.The document encourages NHS trusts in England to carry out an audit to ensure they are offering enough alternatives to single-sex facilities, for instance, gender neutral or single occupancy toilets.Pressures on hospitals mean many have already struggled to keep wards single sex.NHSE data shows that the number of breaches of the previous mixed-sex accommodation guidance has been growing every year since 2021- where members of the opposite sex were placed on a single-sex ward. The most recent figure for August 2026 shows there were 5,520 breaches, compared to 3,853 in June 2025.Sex-based rights charity Sex Matters has welcomed the guidance as a "momentous shift back to reality", but is concerned about how it will be applied. "NHS patient data is a mess, with potentially thousands of trans-identifying people recorded as the opposite sex," CEO Maya Forstater said.Trans rights organisations TransActual and Trans+ Solidarity Alliance have said they are concerned NHS staff will be unclear on how to safely look after trans patients."This guidance will not survive contact with reality in resource-strapped hospitals and will create unworkable operational challenges," they said.The NHS has been at the centre of a number of high-profile arguments over the interpretation of equality law and workplace regulations.In January 2026, Darlington Memorial Hospital was found to have violated the dignity of a group of nurses who complained about a transgender colleague - a biological male who identified as a woman - being allowed to use the female changing rooms. The nurses were told they should change somewhere else if they objected. The tribunal concluded that the trust had indirectly discriminated against them.The nurses are currently seeking £400,000 from the NHS to cover their legal costs.One of the nurses who brought the action, Bethany Hutchison, who is now president of the Darlington Nurses Union, says they welcome the "clear and necessary guidance" from NHSE, but the test will be whether trusts follow it."The Darlington nurses should never have had to take their own employer to court to secure privacy, dignity and lawful single-sex facilities," she said. "Enforcement cannot continue to depend on the courage and personal sacrifice of individual nurses."In Scotland, another employment tribunal found, in December 2025, that a nurse, Sandie Peggie, had been harassed by NHS Fife over its interpretation of rules on single sex spaces. Peggie had complained about a doctor, who was a trans woman, using the female changing rooms. She was suspended after raising concerns. The tribunal dismissed her other claims of discrimination and victimisation. An appeal is under way and expected to reach the courts next year.

schema.headline: Trans people should use hospital spaces according to biological sex, NHS England says

title: Your child wasn't invited to the party - here's how to handle the disappointment
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Being left off the party list is a sad time for little ones but there are ways to helpByJennifer MeierhansIt'
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Being left off the party list is a sad time for little ones but there are ways to helpByJennifer MeierhansIt's around this time of year when children start coming home with party invitations in their school bag. It's exciting and a sign they're making friends as they embark on school life. But what do you do when your child doesn't get an invitation?If your little one has been left off the list, here are some ways to help them cope. Understand it's a very common scenario Image source, Emma PharaohImage caption, Dr Sasha Hall says not being invited to a birthday party is going to happen to our children at some pointEducational and child psychologist Dr Sasha Hall, who's mum to a three-year-old boy and five-year-old girl, says the first thing to understand is that this scenario is "completely normal"."Unfortunately it's going to happen to all our children at some point in our parenting journey," she tells CBeebies Parenting Download.Dr Hall says while it may be tempting to get involved, it is not helpful in the long term."We can't remove all the obstacles, but we can give them the skills to manage," she says. "It's about building their resilience... what skills can we teach rather than change their outcomes?"Comedian, author and mum-of-two Cariad Lloyd says it is a "rough" position for a child to find themselves in. "When they're little, it feels like first love... everything feels so heightened, especially with the party thing. Everyone gets not invited to somebody's party."Plan an alternative activity as a distraction Image caption, Cariad Lloyd and Dr Sasha Hall joined CBeebies Parenting Download Dr Hall suggests planning an alternative activity for your child to focus on instead of the party."Yes, that child said you can't come, but let's find another friend you can do something else with," she says.Lloyd adds that the more the party situation crops up throughout their primary school years, the more you can explain the different outcomes to them."They will be invited to lots of parties and not invited to loads and you'll stop counting them," she says."They will come back and be like 'so-and-so was upset because they're not invited'. And you'll be like, 'oh, do you remember when you were not invited to that one's party?' They all kind of take it in turns so it becomes less dramatic."CBeebies Parenting DownloadHelping children navigate friendshipsExplain it's not about themDr Hall says it's important to explain to your child that the decision to leave them off the list is not about them."There are so many factors at play, especially with five to seven-year-olds, they're too little to have built up any kind of idea that they're naughty, it most likely has nothing to do with your child," she says.Lloyd agrees it's worth explaining possible reasons: "They can't afford to have 20 kids at a party so they're doing six instead and you didn't make the cut."Dr Hall says there could be a myriad of reasons why your child hasn't been invited."It's about the parents' own childhood experience - if they only had a couple of friends at that age they may be happy and comfortable with a smaller party - or they might want a big party in the hope of bringing their child out of their shyness."Acknowledge it will likely blow overDr Hall says parents should remember it is not until children are slightly older that friendships take on a deeper meaning, so what may seem like a big deal now is likely to blow over."Around the age of two is when we start seeing them show an interest in others, but it's still kind of parallel play," she says."And then it's around three to five where they're actually socially motivated to choose preferences. So they might say 'I played with this child today', but it's around about five to seven where those friendships become more stable and that they're really meaningful to the child."She says parents should give children plenty of time and opportunities to form friendships."There's a piece of research that looked at how do adults go from acquaintances to friends and it says it takes 40 to 60 hours - acquaintance to good friend is 200."We then can't assume that because you've gone to soft play and your child has seen that kid twice that therefore you can say that's your friend."For more advice on all aspects of parenting including friendship and shyness go to the CBeebies Parenting YouTube channel., external

schema.headline: Your child wasn't invited to the party - here's how to handle the disappointment

title: Russell Brand accuser says alleged rape left her afraid she may be pregnant
description: Warning - this report contains graphic contentA woman who alleges Russell Brand raped her in a hotel room has said he turned from "camp, friendly and
body: Warning - this report contains graphic contentA woman who alleges Russell Brand raped her in a hotel room has said he turned from "camp, friendly and effeminate" to "monster-like" before the alleged assault.The 51-year-old actor and comedian faces seven charges - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.One of the women told the jury at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday: "He was just dark and arrogant and performing - he was scary, he was demanding."The woman told police she met Brand before he was famous while attending the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth in 1999. She alleges he later raped her.The woman said she was left feeling "dirty" and afraid she may be pregnant in the aftermath of the alleged attack.Before the alleged rape, the woman also said Brand made her take photos of him with his top off, which were shown to the jury.The jury were played a police interview with the woman recorded in 2023, when reporting the alleged crime, before she was called to the witness box on Thursday. The complainant said she and Brand had gone back to a hotel room. She told the police officer she thought Brand "was gay" when they met earlier and she didn't feel like he was "trying it on with her".The woman said she had been in the bathroom, but when she came out "he had like briefs on - and I was like taken aback and shocked. He was prancing around".The complainant alleged Brand told her: "Don't worry, that's how I am."She recalled thinking "what on earth have I got into" when, she claims, a shirtless Brand made her take photos of him before the alleged attack.She was heard telling the officer: "I'm reporting that Russell Brand did rape me."What I'm going to say now - then, I second guessed myself if it was rape because it was so normal."Sorry... he raped me basically - I know that happened. I remember him touching my breasts a lot - while kissing my neck."During the video evidence, Brand watched the TV screen attached to the dock - rarely taking his eyes away. He appeared to be listening attentively and hardly moved his position throughout.Describing the alleged encounter, the woman later told the jury: "He was big, I felt threatened and he's half-naked... I didn't think at that point his intentions were good.""He was the centre of the show, it was like it was back on stage – he wasn't the [same] person I was chatting to."She added: "He just changed suddenly from this... camp, friendly and effeminate to monster-like."The woman recounted to police how Brand acted "like Basil Fawlty when he does his goose steps" before the alleged rape.She told the officer: "I remember him being like an ostrich - like a bird because he was very leggy."I wasn't laughing, I just remember him jumping up and down being silly."The woman said after Brand left the room she was "just sitting there crying and I felt stupid," adding: "In that moment in time I was just shocked."At one point in the police interview, she cried while saying "this was something dirty that had happened".She said she "thought it was my fault", adding that she was "having nightmares" about the possibility of being pregnant.The complainant said she had delayed coming forward because she was worried it would impact her professional life. "I was told if you come out with this, your career is done," she said.Under cross-examination Brand's barrister, Ian Winter KC put it to the complainant that when she first met Brand she welcomed his attention."I welcomed his company, not what followed," the woman replied.He then suggested that she fell under his spell and that she wanted to spend more time with him.The woman replied: "That's incorrect. I did not fall under his spell and I did not find him attractive. "Asked by the defence why she agreed to go back to the hotel room with Brand, she responded: "I'm telling you... I thought he was a gay man, very softly spoken, very effeminate."I felt safe – I felt sexually safe with him. He was very intelligent and that appealed to me, not in a sexual sense. "The woman became tearful a number of times while giving her evidence from the witness box.At one point the judge told the witness to "take a moment, catch your breath", after she became emotional.Brand's barrister later challenged the complainant about why she did not run back into the bathroom or leave the room when she realised Brand had removed some of his clothes.She replied: "What was I supposed to do? Hide in bathroom? Walk out the room? Walk past him? I had no phone, no reception, no idea where I was. Run into the night with him following me?"Referring to photographs she had taken of Brand, she said: "I took those photographs, he told me to take them, he was showing off, he was prancing around... I was scared... I couldn't fight him."I blame myself for allowing him back into my room," the woman said.She was also challenged by the defence barrister about why she didn't report her allegation about Brand to the police in Bournemouth.She said: "I didn't report it as I didn't want anyone to know. I didn't think anyone would believe me."The woman told the jury that after she says she was raped by Brand she blamed herself "in that moment"."I hate that I blamed myself, I shouldn't have to blame myself."She also told jurors: "I regret to this day the error in judgment thinking this man would not rape me.

schema.headline: Russell Brand accuser says alleged rape left her afraid she may be pregnant

title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
description: ByJoshua CheethamThomas Copeland and Alison BenjaminBBC VerifyThe number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz
body: ByJoshua CheethamThomas Copeland and Alison BenjaminBBC VerifyThe number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes.Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts.The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners".Two crew missing after one of Sunday's attacksThe aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby.The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard.Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said.Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated.Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route".Oil shipments stallMiddle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen.About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day.The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August.Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman.These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore.So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships.Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day"."The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added.The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media.Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman.A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard.Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said.Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship.Additional reporting by Becky DaleGraphics by Tom Shiel and Mark Edwards

schema.headline: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow

title: Reform faces questions over candidate vetting after undercover filming
description: Reform UK is facing further questions about its vetting procedures for candidates, after undercover filming broadcast by ITV News, external.In the fil
body: Reform UK is facing further questions about its vetting procedures for candidates, after undercover filming broadcast by ITV News, external.In the film, gathered over the course of a year, an undercover reporter is advised by a local party chairman to delete social media posts supportive of far-right activist Tommy Robinson, before being encouraged to apply to stand to be a councillor for the party.It also shows a former Reform candidate claiming he failed the party's vetting process twice but was still allowed to stand to be a councillor. Reform denies the individual failed vetting in the first place.Reform MP Robert Jenrick said all political parties had "bad apples".Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, he said he "didn't like what I heard in the documentary" but argued that the party had acted quickly, removing or suspending those in the undercover film. "I don't accept this happens any more in Reform than in any other party," he added. In a statement, Reform said that "from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting" but added: "This is the same for all organisations."It follows undercover filming broadcast on Wednesday night, which showed some of Reform's councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language.The party said: "There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases."Reform also accused the ITV investigation of "extreme methods of deception" and using false information to obtain an undercover role in Reform's headquarters.Jenrick said he believed the undercover reporters had wanted to find evidence of party leader Nigel Farage "acting in an inappropriate way" but had not succeeded. Two years ago, Reform leader Nigel Farage vowed to vet candidates more "rigorously", after the party dropped a series of candidates following reports they had made offensive or racist comments.However, the party has continued to face questions over the strength of its vetting processes.Speaking on Thursday, before the latest filming was broadcast, Farage told BBC Look East his party vetted "to a much higher standard than other parties" but "you can't vet for future comments".ITV News says one of its undercover reporters was asked if he would consider standing to be a councillor, after spending time leafleting with Reform activists.He meets with the chairman of a local Reform branch in Chester, Ian Frost, who describes the meeting as "the first stage" of the vetting process.After the reporter says he has previously posted in support of Robinson on social media, Frost advises him to delete the posts."Anything where you've got, things, Tommy Robinson or anything like that, okay, I would delete the account and I'd start again," Frost adds.Farage has said Robinson would not be allowed to join Reform.Frost later suggests the undercover reporter could apply to stand for the party, saying: "You might become a councillor. You might then want to go to the MP route. So, social media, yeah. And apply."Frost told ITV News he thought the reporter was a genuine candidate and gave him the benefit of the doubt. He added that it was not fair to judge people on a single conversation and he had since left Reform for unrelated reasons.In another part of the film, a former Reform candidate - Alex Lomas - claims he failed the party's vetting process twice, including for sharing social media posts from Robinson.However, Lomas says a few days after he failed for the second time he was asked to stand for the party."On my second application, I got declined on the Friday, I got an email from them on the Tuesday saying you've passed vetting," he is recorded as saying."I said, well, I think you better check with your paperwork, mate, because I've just failed on Friday. Now, you're saying I've passed it, I've not changed anything. "And then I got a phone call a few days later. Hi, will you stand for Reform UK? I'm like, yeah okay."He stood for Reform in local elections in Oldham in May but did not win a seat on the council.The BBC has not been able to contact Lomas and he did not respond to requests for comment from ITV News.Reform denies Lomas failed vetting in the first place.ITV's undercover report also shows Farage ruling a controversial mayoral candidate Dr Chris Parry – who said the then Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy should go home to the Caribbean – should be made to apologise, but not stand down.In a conversation at Reform's headquarters, the party's director of communications Ed Sumner suggests Farage is "protecting" Parry.In response Farage says: "It's showing a bit of sorrow."In a separate conversation several weeks earlier, where Farage was not present, Sumner is recorded saying Parry is "clearly a racist" and "needs to go".After apologising to Lammy in January, Parry was allowed to remain Reform's mayoral candidate in Hampshire and the Solent until he was later suspended in March "pending investigation", following comments about a Jewish voluntary patrol service.Parry told the BBC there was never an investigation and he has since left the party.He said: "I would urge people to go back to the original contexts and tweets to see what was said and why. They related to reparations and failures by the police and government. "They will see I always exercise my right to criticise anyone in power or the public eye, whom I judge to be acting against the interests of the British people."In the report, Reform UK MP Sarah Pochin is filmed telling the undercover reporter that the party needed "women press officers"."Thy are so chauvinistic... They just exclude you if you are a woman. There's a bit of a male issue going on."Asked about her comments, Jenrick said Pochin was a "valued colleague" but added: "It is not my experience that the party has problems of that kind."Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "These latest shocking and deeply disturbing revelations go right to the top of Reform UK. "Nigel Farage needs to wake up and realise the buck stops with him. He also must urgently explain why he allegedly stood by a blatant racist instead of kicking him out of his party."Time and again Farage has had every opportunity to demonstrate leadership and get Reform's house in order and every single time he has failed."

schema.headline: Reform faces questions over candidate vetting after undercover filming

title: Newspaper headlines: Healey's 'tax raid on banks' and Brand 'topless monster'
description: "Healey plans tax raid on banks", declares the Daily Telegraph, external. According to the Guardian, one option understood, external to be under discu
body: "Healey plans tax raid on banks", declares the Daily Telegraph, external. According to the Guardian, one option understood, external to be under discussion for the Budget would be to reverse cuts to the bank surcharge made by the former Conservative chancellor, Jeremy Hunt. The paper says this would raise upwards of £2bn a year. But banks have told the Telegraph that increasing the surcharge would cost the economy £20bn. The Treasury says decisions on tax are for the chancellor to set out.The i Paper reports that there will be a "double" rise, external in energy bills next year. Forecasts suggest the annual price cap will go up by £276 in January. According to the i Paper, the chancellor is also unlikely to recommend keeping VAT off electricity bills beyond March."Dumb & dumber", is the Daily Mail's headline, external take on the government's reforms for schools in England. The paper draws attention to plans from the education secretary, Lucy Powell, that speaking skills will become just as important as reading and writing in GCSE assessments. The Mail's sketch writer, Quentin Letts, says in a speech about the importance of clear communication, Powell was "as clear as public-lavatory glass".Europe's biggest salmon producers are beginning to feed chicken to their fish, in a move the Financial Times says, external breaks a "longstanding taboo in the hunt for cheap protein". Consumers are said to have found the practice "unnatural", but one expert quoted in the FT says "the market seems to be more ready". Salmon producers also claim using chicken cuts costs and carbon emissions.Much is made of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's first public engagement together since returning to the UK. Metro says Meghan was "beaming in burgundy", external in Nottingham, while the Daily Mirror declares that her husband was "happy as HARRY"., external "Crowds treat Sussexes like royalty", is headline in the Times, external. "The obvious question", the Daily Mail asks, "is what can the Palace do about it?" , externalThe answer: "very little."

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: Healey's 'tax raid on banks' and Brand 'topless monster'

title: Banks say Healey planning to increase tax on their profits in Budget
description: Chancellor John Healey is planning to increase taxes on the bank sector, senior banking executives have told the BBC.Healey has described banks as par
body: Chancellor John Healey is planning to increase taxes on the bank sector, senior banking executives have told the BBC.Healey has described banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, but leaders in the sector have said it will be "on the menu" at the Budget in two weeks' time.The biggest four banks collectively made about £15bn profit in the first six months of this year, and trade unions have called for them to face additional taxes.The trade body for the banking sector, UK Finance, warned "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode".What is the Budget and what could be in it?The UK's biggest banks and building societies currently pay a surcharge of 3% on top of the baseline 25% rate of corporation tax - a tax on profits. They also pay a  levy on the assets held on their balance sheets.The sector contributed nearly £40bn to the Treasury last year, if income tax on employees is factored in.The bank levy generated £1.4bn last year and the surcharge a further £1.2bn.There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector.The 3% surcharge was reduced from 8% under Rishi Sunak, at the same time as he raised corporation tax from 19% to 25%. Returning the surcharge to its previous level could raise around £2bn a year.The bank levy is a tax on banks not related to their profits, which charges them based instead on the size of their balance sheets. It currently charges 0.1% on outstanding short-term loans and 0.05% on longer-dated loans, although mortgages are excluded from the calculation.In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth.Sir Philip Augar, an author and former banker in the City of London, told the BBC's Today programme there was "room for a moderate increase" in taxes on the sector that could raise up to £3bn a year.He said lenders were enjoying "booming conditions", benefiting from higher interest rates which boost their profits.Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which banks lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.Sir Philip added that when the banking sector "hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out - when it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment".He said banks cannot simultaneously be "too big to fail and too big to tax".Paul Nowak, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, which represents trade unions, said the majority of bank workers "are not fat cats or city high rollers", adding that "we want a successful financial services industry in the UK"."But if the chancellor does ask the Banks to pay a fairer share of tax in the Budget, that's 100% the right call," he added.Banks were pleased to have avoided being targeted at the last Budget, given the large profits they have made in recent years. There is another option that has been discussed with Treasury officials. Currently banks can use losses from the past to offset against profits - thereby reducing their tax bill in any given year. Lloyds in particular has been a beneficiary of this policy, as large losses from the financial crisis have been used to lower tax bills ever since.Some analysts and bank executives have pushed the idea of a moratorium on this practice for a few years, which would yield an estimated extra £1bn per year for the Treasury. That would provide a windfall while being "a lot more bearable", in the words of one bank executive.It would also spare foreign banks from an additional hit, including JP Morgan, whose chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned that the UK already has one of the highest tax burdens on banks in the world. He warned that adding further sector-specific taxes could discourage investment and damage competitiveness.However, industry leaders say any form of tax rise that hits UK banks and exempts foreign banks' operations in the UK would be hard to square with the government's push to back British business.

schema.headline: Banks say Healey planning to increase tax on their profits in Budget

title: London suburban housing project wins top UK architecture award
description: Williamson told the BBC that until he went to study architecture he lived in a council estate in the East Midlands, "and every time I go back there al
body: Williamson told the BBC that until he went to study architecture he lived in a council estate in the East Midlands, "and every time I go back there all the council houses have been sold off, they're in private hands. "Which in a way can be a good thing - we're in a homeowning democracy - but the sad thing is they haven't been replaced. "Every time I go back - without getting too emotional - I think 'where would we have lived?' "So to me that's why this particular project was important. I think a lot of people from that sort of background live in terrible accommodation - temporary accommodation which isn't safe or secure. "These houses are fantastic and they're part of a mixed scheme so it's got a fantastic feel to it. "For me it was a very inspirational, emotional, part of the process."Duggan, who was brought up in south-west London, said the scheme "challenged conventional suburban housing layouts centred on roads, private gardens and clearly defined front and back spaces".Winding paths and planting weave between the blocks, connecting them and linking shared outdoor spaces.She said she wanted it to be a public space people felt they could belong to."Housing needs to be progressive. People who live in the building have access to green space, allotments."The site fronts onto Lion Green Road, with low-rise green belt housing set on higher ground to the south and traditional suburban streets to the north.

schema.headline: London suburban housing project wins top UK architecture award

title: Is women's health content being 'shadowbanned'?
description: When Irene Breen got a notification in January 2025 that Instagram was removing adverts for her company's pregnancy pillows, she was confused. What wa
body: When Irene Breen got a notification in January 2025 that Instagram was removing adverts for her company's pregnancy pillows, she was confused. What was so offensive about a pillow?She was later told on a call with Meta that the problem was the word "pregnancy"."We had to scrub the word from our entire website… from the product name," Breen said. "We had to remove all our URLs which had pregnancy in them and rename them all."The restrictions were eventually lifted but, she said, it took 10 months of conversations with Instagram's parent company Meta - by which time her business had suffered a significant financial hit.Meta, which also owns Facebook, declined to comment on specific cases, but told the BBC that while businesses can run adverts that promote wellness, sexual health and reproductive products and services, there are restrictions to avoid users across countries and cultures having a negative experience. It's not just businesses taking out paid adverts who claim their content has been unfairly restricted.Women's health creators and charities have told us their content has been removed, had sensitivity filters added, or had its reach suppressed - a practice known as "shadowbanning".The campaign group CensHERship monitors claims that women's health content is being suppressed. In a report last month, it surveyed nearly 200 creators, clinical providers, health brands, charities, and educators - 96% of whom said they had experienced restrictions in some form.CensHERship found the number of respondents self-censoring as a result of shadowbanning had gone up, from 53% in 2025 to 65% this year. This includes using euphemistic terms such as "seggs" instead of "sex", using asterisks or emojis, and avoiding certain topics altogether.CensHERship co-founder Clio Wood said this was "really damaging", because "women's health historically has been surrounded by shame and guilt… and we are just reinforcing [that]".Are told the BBC that platforms' policies "tend to be incredibly broad, whereby more often than not, nudity is conflated with sexual activity".And this ultimately hurts audiences, Wood said."We talk to so many people who say, 'The only reason I found out about my vulval cancer was because Eve Appeal posted about those symptoms, and then I researched it and could ask my doctor the right questions'," she said.But Wood said that, since starting CensHERship in 2024, she has noticed that social media companies "can see this is something that they need to engage on now."."It's all very well the policy saying XYZ content is allowed, but if the algorithm is still flagging all of that content and suppressing it, that's where the problem comes in," she said."I think within the platforms those departments are very siloed - so what we would love is for those conversations to be much more holistic."

title: They fled Russia, but the West sent them back
description: Russian security services were waiting when the flight landed in Moscow in December. On board were Russians the US had deported, including activists d
body: Russian security services were waiting when the flight landed in Moscow in December. On board were Russians the US had deported, including activists denied political asylum."It was unbelievably frightening. My knees were shaking with fear," says Katya, one of the deportees. We have changed her name to protect her identity, as she remains in Russia.Katya had left Russia and claimed asylum in the US two years earlier.When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, many countries publicly welcomed fleeing Russians. But more than four years later, attitudes have hardened. The numbers of anti-war Russians forcibly returned from Western countries is rising, and Katya's experience highlights the potential risks they face.US authorities rejected her application for asylum, after she said she had provided evidence that she had taken part in protests and was a member of an opposition movement.In Moscow, Katya says officers from the FSB security service handed all the male deportees military papers, requiring them to register with the local enlistment office, from where men are often sent to the war in Ukraine. Another passenger on the flight and an activist confirmed her account.The officers interrogated her, and many others, for several hours."At one point, they found incriminating information on my phone," says Katya, "Their faces changed in a second. I was very afraid that they would simply bundle me off somewhere."Katya was eventually released and allowed to stay with relatives. But she says police continue to call her and visit her at home."I feel as if I'm in a cage, like in a zoo," she says, "Whenever I see a police car, I feel terrified and start thinking, "What if they're coming for me?"Katya showed the BBC documents and photographs confirming her story, which matches accounts from other deportees.Removals from the US rose from 222 in 2023 to more than 1,200 in 2025, amid a wider increase in deportations under President Donald Trump's second term. Activists say Russian deportees included dissidents and Russian army deserters, some of whom were imprisoned or sent to war after returning to Russia.One such case is Leonid Melekhin, an anti-war activist who sought asylum in the US after being arrested at protests in Russia. He had posted photographs of Russian President Vladimir Putin online with the message "Putin: murderer, fascist, usurper". After being deported back home last year, Melekhin was charged with "justifying terrorism" and sentenced to six years in prison."We have several examples of people who got eight years in prison when they crossed the [Russian] border," says Andrei Pivovarov, from Russia's exiled opposition Anti-War Committee.And deportations are taking place from Europe too. His organisation has changed its advice to dissidents escaping Russia: the EU is no longer safe, it is better to seek refuge elsewhere.Germany has sharply increased the number of Russian nationals it deports. Seven were sent back in 2023, rising to more than 110 in 2025, according to German government figures. More than 21,000 Russians sought asylum in Germany between 2022 and 2025, but the proportion of positive decisions fell from 29% in 2023 to just 6.8% in the first eleven months of 2025."Protection is only granted if there is an actual, well-founded fear of persecution," Germany's migration and asylum agency, BAMF, told the BBC.Last year, Berlin suspended its humanitarian visa programme for Russians, and across the EU, the proportion of Russian applicants granted some form of asylum protection fell from 23% in 2024 to around 17% in the first nine months of 2025, according to EU data.Russian opposition activists fleeing repression have become caught up in a wider crackdown on immigration, as governments across Europe and the US toughen rules amid political pressure over high numbers of irregular migrants and asylum applications, as well as over security concerns.Western governments are "focused on limiting humanitarian programmes and asylum seekers", says lawyer Anastasia Burakova, founder of rights group Kovcheg (Ark), which helps anti-war Russians leave the country. The clampdown is "in response to public concerns and rising support for right-wing populist parties", she adds.Following a negative asylum decision, Russian nationals are often given the chance to leave independently, but a rising number are being forcibly returned to Russia, usually escorted via third countries.Several Russian activists in exile told the BBC that immigration officials had told them they faced "no danger" in Russia, and that officials often lacked an adequate understanding of the risks that activists face."I tried to explain that if they sent me back, I would be put in prison, or sent to war where I'd be killed," explains former soldier Artyom, who deserted from the Russian Army in 2022 after officers threatened to send him to Ukraine. "They just didn't believe me."He says he provided US authorities with proof that a criminal investigation had been opened against him back in Russia for desertion. But he was put on a deportation flight back to Moscow via Egypt."I was preparing for death," says the former soldier, "I was thinking, 'how can I die without it being painful?'".Back in Moscow, Artyom was held in a military detention facility but managed to escape. He is now in hiding abroad."Another country could investigate me better and give me asylum. Why didn't they give me that chance? Instead they deported me specifically to Russia," says the deserter. "It ruined my life."The US Department of Homeland Security told the BBC: "All illegal aliens receive due process. If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them."The asylum clampdown comes as repression inside Russia has reached "an unprecedented level", according to Nobel Prize-winning Russian human rights group Memorial. Their list of political prisoners grew from 803 to 1,265 during 2025, a record increase.The Russian Embassy in London did not respond to a request for comment.Anti-war activist Mikhail says he and his wife Dasha are awaiting deportation from Finland "any day". Their names have been changed to protect their identity, as Mikhail fears for relatives back home.Russian authorities blocked his social media accounts over anti-war posts, and police visited his mother and accused him of spreading "fake information".Dasha is a Jehovah's Witness, an organisation banned as "extremist" in Russia. The couple provided Finnish authorities with evidence, seen by the BBC, including a video of Russian police telling his mother that more than 300 posts had violated Russian law. A single post can result in a long prison sentence.The Finnish Immigration Service has rejected their asylum request five times, deciding there is "no reasonable basis to believe" the couple would face serious rights violations if returned."We're sitting here and someone could knock on our door at any moment, take us to the Russian border and simply hand us over to Russian officers," says Mikhail. "We fear for our lives!""We came to Finland for help, and they're refusing us," he adds. "My wife cries constantly."Amnesty International, which is supporting the couple, says they could face a "real risk" of detention, prosecution, imprisonment and torture if returned.The Finnish Immigration Service said all asylum decisions were based on international refugee law standards, and the share of Russian citizens receiving asylum was in line with EU averages.For Mikhail and Dasha, the threat of deportation comes as more Russians may be considering leaving.There are rumours that Vladimir Putin may announce a new wave of mobilisation to boost the ranks of his army in Ukraine, which the Kremlin denies. The last mobilisation in 2022 prompted hundreds of thousands of Russians to flee, many to ex-Soviet states such as Armenia and Georgia.Anastasia Burakova's organisation says requests for help from Russians wanting to leave rose tenfold in August compared with May. For those now looking to escape, the question is whether the West will offer them refuge — or send them back.

schema.headline: They fled Russia, but the West sent them back

title: Same-day test helps doctors detect hidden infections in critically ill children
description: "The fact that they had a test there available to her was paramount.  It saved her life," said Stacey."It's a miracle she's here and we're extremely g
body: "The fact that they had a test there available to her was paramount.  It saved her life," said Stacey."It's a miracle she's here and we're extremely grateful for that," added Willow's dad, Russ.With the right treatment, Willow was eventually able to recover from her infection, but needed several months in hospital. She is one of many patients at the children's hospital to benefit from the new type of testing.During a study in 2024-5 metagenomic testing was used on 122 critically ill children in the paediatric intensive care unit (ICU) at GOSH.The results have now been published in the Lancet Microbe.Metagenomic testing analyses all genetic material in a sample and can detect thousands of different pathogens. By contrast, the most common method of identifying bacteria is by trying to culture them in Petri dishes, a technology that has been used since Victorian times.Another test, PCR, can identify viruses and some bacteria, but doctors need to specify what they are trying to detect.Metagenomics testing at GOSH was able to identify around nine in 10 bacteria and viruses and all fungi in samples.In a quarter of cases, the results influenced prescribing decisions, including starting, stopping or changing an antibiotic.Dr Sam Ray, consultant in paediatric intensive care medicine at GOSH and co-author of the study said traditional testing required clinicians to make an educated guess about which infection they were looking for. "The study has helped us to spot infections we would have missed, get children on the right treatment and stop antibiotics when we know they aren't going to work."Removing unnecessary treatment is incredibly important for the fight against growing antimicrobial resistance."Metagenomic testing at GOSH also detected 50 organisms not identified by routine diagnostics, meaning it could play an early warning role against new infections.Dr Julianne Brown, head of the GOSH Metagenomics Service and co-senior author of the study said the new testing was being gradually rolled out to around 30 intensive care units across the UK treating both adults and children."It could be a powerful tool for identifying new infections that pose a pandemic threat," she added."In the future, if there was to be a new mystery pathogen that could be a cause of the next pandemic, we would detect that very quickly and put the right measures in place."The project at GOSH builds on trials at Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Trust which first used metagenomics to test for respiratory infections in adult patients.

schema.headline: Same-day test helps doctors detect hidden infections in critically ill children

title: I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
description: Jess Bacon does all her clothes shopping online. As a plus-size woman, she finds the size ranges available in stores unreliable. "The sizing in store
body: Jess Bacon does all her clothes shopping online. As a plus-size woman, she finds the size ranges available in stores unreliable. "The sizing in store is notoriously bad. I find it quite demoralising in store," she says."The average size woman in the UK is a size 14 or a size 16. I think a lot of people just don't feel seen or represented," says the 29-year-old from Peterborough.Jess, a culture journalist and author, finds shopping online "much quicker than going into a store, paying for parking, trying things on".And she feels posting back items that don't fit is less hassle than returning in store, while frequent visits to her local post office give her "more of a community connection".Jess notes Primark is one of the few High Street retailers where plus-size people can shop. In her experience, Primark stores usually stock up to a size 22.But soon she'll have the option of staying home even for this - as, after years of holding out, Primark now plans to launch a home delivery service in Britain.Even throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, when shops were closed, Primark didn't offer the ability to shop online. In 2022 it launched a click-and-collect service, but shoppers still had to travel for their purchases.The retailer has not said when it expects to launch the service, but has bought a warehouse in Sheffield to enable it to ship products to homes.Analysts say the decision shows Primark is facing major challenges from ultra-fast-fashion brands such as Shein.Julie Palmer, a retail analyst, is not surprised that Primark has finally moved into home deliveries as it has evidently recognised that "online sales bring scale".However, she says a shop's returns policy for online purchases can "make or break" it. Many brands offer hassle-free returns, which Palmer says Primark must match in order to compete. "Shoppers want them to be free, simple and quick. That means a generous window, lots of drop-off options and refunds that land within days, not weeks."When a policy is clunky or slow, customers remember it and shop elsewhere next time."But returns are expensive for retailers. Some, like Asos, have started charging a fee if customers make frequent returns.This is a balancing act, Palmer says, "because a fee can easily push a customer to a competitor"."Most retailers that charge still offer free returns in store, which is a deliberate way to get people through the door and hopefully spending again."

schema.headline: I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online

title: Sparks fly at the Celebrity Traitors round table and a 'terrifying' death march
description: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the fifth episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.Things are hotting up a bit in the castle,
body: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the fifth episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.Things are hotting up a bit in the castle, not least for Ross Kemp, who doesn't seem to be enjoying it very much. "I'm quite angry," he said, his brow furrowing even more than usual. "I've suffered at the hands of the traitors and now they've put heat on me, so I'm quite angry about that," he said. "They're using me like a donkey."Clearly they aren't hitching rides on him at the seaside - that would be another show entirely - he's referring to them pointing the finger of suspicion at him by making him stand out when he doesn't want to. Firstly they kept the former EastEnders star and documentary maker above ground at the grave-digging task, sparing him from being buried. In this episode, he was one of four celebrities who had to sit alone in a tomb, before one of them was murdered.This was intended to get tongues wagging about him, deflecting suspicion away from the actual traitors. Joanne McNally was convinced enough by this to say: "The vibe with Ross is off. His eyes do not close. "He has not blinked since we've been here. He is giving cyborgs."Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in UncloakedComic James Acaster, possibly the most reluctant traitor in recent memory, accurately called killing off Beckett a "chaos murder". "This is a bunch of faithful who read into everything," he said. "They go, why did this happen? And with this murder, there's no answer, and they won't suspect it's us."More accurately, he should perhaps have said: "They won't suspect me or Maya," given only two-thirds of this tactic worked.Meanwhile, the task for this episode made some of the celebrities quite jumpy. This was despite it not involving being buried alive, drinking stinky water or diving down an old toilet, all of which wouldn't have been out of place on I'm A Celebrity, Get Me Out of Here. This episode's death parade saw them having to solve puzzles to avoid being seized and held captive by guards looking like Skeletor, from He-Man and the Masters of the Universe."That is genuinely terrifying," said Pinnock as the marchers approached them on the edge of a forest. "We are literally in a horror film."Michael Sheen took each puzzle as an opportunity to flex his acting muscles, using his finest Shakespearean actor's voice to bellow out the instructions to everyone else. He should have grabbed one of the death marchers to do a quick burst of Hamlet. The celebrities were victorious though, winning all the prize money for charity, and the task ended with Kemp and James Blunt using flints to spark a flame, igniting some gunpowder to hold the death marchers at bay. At the end of the task, players captured by the death marchers were held in a cage until the round table. This included all three traitors - Hannah Fry, Maya Jama and James Acaster - as well as Ranganathan, Jerry Hall and McNally.Oops, bad move. This left a traitor-free zone at the castle, where theories could fly without the traitors trying to derail them. By the time everyone was reunited at the round table, traitor shade was being thrown at several celebrities. Kemp firstly had to defend himself, which he did by saying: "In my defence, I would say if I was picked to be a traitor, I wouldn't have been so paralysed on the first day about the hat [where he thought he was killed in plain sight]."And the grave thing, I don't think it would be traitorous behaviour to get everybody out before you start looking for the money, so I would say that in my defence."This seemed to work, before James Blunt was briefly questioned. But Fry - an actual traitor - came in for the most flak. YouTuber King Kenny swooped, saying: "There's no surprise that I'm going to be talking to you, Hannah. I just don't understand, how are you still here?"Because when I think about it, as a traitor, you'd be one of the first people that I would get out. But also, as the traitor, you'd be extremely good because you're very smart."He wasn't wrong, and this ignited the growing chorus of celebrities who also suspected Fry.The mathematician tried to defend herself, saying: "I've been sort of doomed from the beginning because either I was going to be killed by the traitors or, as has happened, if I don't get killed by traitors, the faithful are going to suspicious of me."When votes were cast, the vast majority were for Fry. Even her fellow traitors turned on her - both Jama and Acaster voted for her, to ensure they looked like faithfuls. "I came in here with absolutely one job and one job only on my mind, which was to catch traitors," she said before she was banished. "And I calculated every conceivable scenario except for the one that actually unfolded."This was because she was of course recruited mid-way through the series.She later added: "My fellow traitors, they had to vote for me. It was so clearly going in that direction. You know what? I didn't choose the traitor life, but oh my goodness me, that was so much fun."Back in the turret, despite comic Joe Lycett's desperate efforts to be recruited, Kenny was chosen as the next traitor, because he had been such a good faithful at the round table.  He even gleefully galloped round the castle with Miranda Hart and Sebastian "Bash" Croft after they caught Fry. That was quite an unexpected sight.

schema.headline: Sparks fly at the Celebrity Traitors round table and a 'terrifying' death march

title: Mother of Henry Nowak killer could be deported
description: The mother of murderer Vickrum Digwa could be in line for deportation from the UK, the Home Office has signalled.Kiran Kaur, 53, was jailed for three
body: The mother of murderer Vickrum Digwa could be in line for deportation from the UK, the Home Office has signalled.Kiran Kaur, 53, was jailed for three years in July for removing the knife used by her son, Vickrum Digwa, to kill student Henry Nowak from the crime scene.However Kaur, who spent several months on remand, could serve less than half of her sentence and be freed around the anniversary of Mr Nowak's death under the Government's early release scheme, ITV News reported., externalThe Home Office and Ministry of Justice declined to comment on individual cases, but said: "We will always seek to deport foreign criminals at the first opportunity."Kaur, who is an Indian national, could be eligible for the government's deportation scheme.She is also appealing against her sentence, with a hearing scheduled at the Court of Appeal on 5 November.Kaur's son Digwa was jailed for life with a minimum term of 21 years on 1 June for the murder of the 18-year-old student, after falsely claiming Mr Nowak had racially abused him in Southampton on 3 December.Some 5,000 prisoners are scheduled to be released in stages over the next year, down from 6,000 after ministers intervened to exempt rapists and the most serious child sex offenders.Ministers say the expanded early release scheme is needed to prevent the justice system from collapsing, after a summer when the issue dominated news headlines.Some 650 criminals were this week released from prisons around the country under the scheme, less than two weeks after 700 were set free early.The Home Office said: "Our thoughts remain with the family and friends of Henry Nowak, whose life was cruelly cut short in a horrific act of violence."

schema.headline: Mother of Henry Nowak killer could be deported

title: Met needs to move away from criminalising sex workers, officers say after Levy failings
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByDaniel De SimoneInvestigations correspondent and Amy JohnstonReporting fromLondonThe Met need to move away from criminalis
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByDaniel De SimoneInvestigations correspondent and Amy JohnstonReporting fromLondonThe Met need to move away from criminalising women involved in street sex work in the wake of the Simon Levy case, officers have told the BBC.Levy, a convicted sex offender, was left to kill two women and rape another - all of whom were vulnerable and sometimes engaged in street sex work - due to a series of failings, including by the force.Now the Met is piloting a new two-officer female team in north London to engage with street sex workers, in a bid to improve trust and encourage them to report crimes committed against them.The Levy case exposed grave failings in policing and also the inherent tension in its approach to street sex workers.Sex work is legal in the UK, excluding Northern Ireland, but related activities like soliciting for clients in public places - known as street sex work - working together, or brothel keeping, pimping and advertising sexual services are all illegal.Street sex workers are also often targeted by police using anti-social behaviour powers.Many women who require protection naturally fear arrest and do not trust officers to investigate violence.On patrol with officers who run new Met schemeThe BBC joined a patrol with the two plain-clothed female officers who run the new Met scheme, Operation Amicus.They described hearing about endemic levels of male violence against the women they have met, who come from a cohort of 80 women in the area identified as involved in street-based sex work."Every single one has reported something," one of the officers said, "whether they've been raped, they've been punched - they've been attacked in some way, shape or form."Image caption, The Met is piloting a new two-officer female team in north London to engage with street sex workersThe officers, whom the BBC agreed not to name, said several women have been too scared to report abuse to the police.The officers described encountering an appalling situation in which women are repeatedly attacked by men but think the police cannot be trusted to help.Some women "expect to be raped and sexually assaulted by customers - it's just become the norm, so [they think] what is the point in reporting [it]", one of the officers said.The new team added that they were trying to help the women to formally report crimes.'They're just trying to survive'"Once they report one and they realise they're being listened to, they then start to report the next one because they know that somebody's [going] to turn up and somebody's going to listen and [they're] going to be taken seriously."The officers the BBC spoke to said the Met needs to move away from criminalising women involved in street sex work – saying it's "not fair" when "they're just trying to survive".They said they were also aware of concerns by residents about sex work in their streets and the need to tackle organised crime.Image caption, Simon Levy, from Tottenham, was given a whole-life term in August Levy, who was given a whole-life term in August, sexually assaulted women at random on London's public transport network, as well as elsewhere. He now has convictions for attacking 13 women he encountered on the Tube and trains, as well as at music events and even in prison.He also targeted vulnerable women involved in street sex work.He killed Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo in March 2025 and Sheryl Wilkins five months later.Image source, Met PoliceImage caption, Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo and Sheryl Wilkins were both murdered by LevyPrior to their murders, Levy had raped a third woman, in January 2025. The rape survivor told police what had happened while she was being arrested by Met officers for allegedly breaching a community banning order.But the Met didn't properly engage with her and eventually closed the rape case. It was only re-opened when Levy went on to murder Valencia-Trujillo and Wilkins, which took place in the same section of a car park where he had raped the surviving victim.The survivor later said in a statement "nobody ever listened to me" and that the police who interviewed her had spoken to her "like a child".The Met and the Crown Prosecution Service have apologised over a series of decisions that left Levy free to roam the streets.Supt Rob Gibbs said the new team is "an acknowledgement that we needed to change the way in which we were working" and move away from criminalising sex work."Women get stuck in the criminal justice system" for minor offences, he said - and this leads to "more sex working and actually we need to break that cycle".Gibbs added that women involved in street-based sex work were at the "most harsh end of violence against women and girls".Image caption, Supt Rob Gibbs says the new team is "an acknowledgement that we needed to change the way in which we were working"While on patrol, the BBC met a woman we are calling Alice to protect her identity.She told us most women she knows who are homeless and engage in sex work in Tottenham, north London, have not reported assaults for fear of the police and being arrested themselves.She said two men have attacked her in separate incidents this year, including a man who violently assaulted her after she declined to take his money and sell him sex a few months ago."I was scared to contact the police," she said. "When I went to the hospital I begged the doctors, 'please don't phone the police because I'll get arrested'."Alice said she first met the Met's female sex-worker liaison team when she was attacked by another man after falling asleep in a lift to her mum's apartment."They came and said, 'look, we're not here to arrest you, get you in trouble, we're here to support you'," Alice said.'Women describe absolute terror from the police'The Met says the new team has already improved safeguarding and increased reports of rape and sexual offences, as well as improving information sharing to identify "the most dangerous perpetrators of violence against women and girls".However, the English Collective of Prostitutes (ECP) - which advocates for decriminalisation of sex workers - said that previous police clear-up operations on organised crime in London and around the country have led to a longstanding history of police prioritising prosecuting sex workers, rather than investigating male violence against them.Laura Watson, a caseworker for the ECP, said a "very intense and aggressive police crackdown" in north London had led to "quite aggressive arrests of women" in Enfield and Haringey."In some cases, closure zones and antisocial behaviour orders which banned women from entire areas in some cases" led to "mass criminalisation because women were breaching those orders".She said "women really describe absolute terror from the police, running up and down the road, running away from the police".Most street sex workers are "mothers working to feed themselves and their children", she told us.Image caption, Laura Watson, a caseworker from the English Collective of Prostitutes, said a crackdown in north London had led to "quite aggressive arrests of women" Prof Kate Brown, from the University of York, whose research focuses on policing interventions with sex workers, said creating such teams was not in itself a solution."Our research shows that sex work liaison officers can make a real difference to safety and access to justice, but only when they are designed and delivered in the right way," she said.Her research centre is working with 12 police forces out of 43 in England and Wales, to safely implement sex worker liaison teams.But she said these teams "cannot fix a system that continues to police and criminalise sex workers" and that "decriminalisation is the best way to deliver safety and justice" for them.The Met said that if the team was "successful in improving confidence within the community", then this approach would be "rolled out across the force".A Home Office spokesperson said: "Our commitment to halving violence against women and girls within a decade includes tackling the serious exploitation and abuse associated with prostitution."We expect the police to treat all victims of offences with dignity, and every investigation to be conducted thoroughly. We also continue to work with NGOs and charities to ensure women and girls at risk of sexual exploitation are protected."

schema.headline: Met needs to move away from criminalising sex workers, officers say after Levy failings
